subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 13 periods = 650 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 10h 50min

periods.activity_title: Force as a Vector: Magnitude, Direction, and Effect
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing force arrows on a ball for kicking, batting, and squeezing scenarios

time_bands.activity: Students are shown a ball on the desk. The teacher asks: what could you do to change where it is or how it moves? Students call out actions (push, kick, throw, squeeze). The teacher lists these on the board and asks: what do all these actions have in common? Students discuss in pairs and share — arriving at the idea that they all involve a push or pull applied to the object.

The teacher introduces force as a vector quantity requiring both magnitude and direction. Using a diagram of a ball on the board, students draw arrows to show what happens if the force on the ball is doubled in magnitude, then kept the same magnitude but reversed in direction. The teacher connects this to earlier work on displacement and velocity as vector quantities from Chapter 4, asking students to articulate why force must be a vector and what would change if only the direction of a kick changed.

Students work through the Think It Over scenario: a canoeist pushes water backward and the canoe moves forward. In small groups, students (a) draw force-arrow diagrams showing the direction of the paddle force and the direction of canoe motion, and (b) reason about which canoe — empty or passenger-carrying — reaches higher speed with the same paddle force, and why. Groups report their reasoning; the teacher draws out the idea that the effect of a force depends on both its magnitude and the object it acts on.

The teacher introduces the SI unit newton (N), lowercase spelling, and symbol N. Students write two or three sentences explaining in their own words: what a force is, what two properties specify it, and what the SI unit is. Pairs exchange and check each other's explanations for completeness.

Whole-class quick check: the teacher poses three rapid scenarios on the board — a bat hitting a ball (direction changes), a hand squeezing a lemon (shape changes), a pushed car speeding up (speed changes). Students identify which property of force (magnitude, direction, or both) is responsible in each case and give a one-sentence justification.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's study of forces, so orient students to the idea that force is not just a push or pull in everyday language but a precisely defined physical quantity with magnitude and direction. Watch for the common error that only moving objects experience forces — students may not recognise that a squeezed lemon or a stationary object being held also involves forces. A useful probing question for the canoe Think It Over is: 'If direction of paddle stroke reversed, what changes about the canoe's motion?' — this sharpens the vector understanding.

periods.activity_title: Measuring Force with a Spring Balance: From Weight to Any Force
periods.section_anchor: 6.1.1 Measuring the magnitude of a force
materials: spring balance (at least one per group of four)
assorted small objects of known or estimable weight
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure or board diagram of a spring balance showing scale, hook, and reading position

time_bands.activity: Each group receives a spring balance. Students examine it: locate the hook, the scale, and the zero mark. The teacher asks: what quantity does this instrument measure? Students share prior knowledge — they have used spring balances to measure weight. The teacher asks: what is weight, physically? Students articulate that weight is the force with which Earth pulls an object downward.

Groups apply forces to the spring balance in different ways: hang an object from the hook and read weight; press a finger against the hook horizontally and read; have one student pull the hook with a rubber band at an angle. For each, students record (a) the reading in newtons, (b) the direction in which the force was applied. The teacher asks: does the spring balance only measure weight, or any force? Students conclude that it measures the magnitude of any applied force, regardless of direction, by converting force into extension.

The teacher explains the scale of forces: the smallest forces humans can directly feel are in the order of millinewtons; specialised experiments detect forces as small as yoctonewtons (10⁻²⁴ N). Students are asked to express 1 millinewton in standard notation and to estimate how many yoctonewtons equal 1 millinewton — practising scientific notation while anchoring the scale of measurement instruments.

Students construct a brief explanation (three to four sentences) addressing: how a spring balance works as a force-measuring instrument, why weight is a force, and what the unit of measurement is. They annotate a quick sketch of the spring balance, labelling the hook, scale, and the force being measured.

Class discussion: the teacher asks — could you measure the force of a magnet attracting a paper clip using a spring balance? How? Students reason through the procedure, reinforcing that the spring balance measures any force magnitude, not just gravitational weight.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that force has magnitude and direction, this unit focuses entirely on how magnitude is quantified using a spring balance. A frequent confusion is that the spring balance measures mass rather than force — students should articulate explicitly that the reading in newtons represents the gravitational force (weight) when an object hangs from the hook, and any applied force in other uses. Encourage students to read the scale from directly in front to avoid parallax error, which is a useful practical habit to name here.

periods.activity_title: Net Force from Multiple Forces: Balanced and Unbalanced Configurations
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of a block with force arrows in three configurations matching Example 6.1

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the tug-of-war scenario: two equally matched teams pull a rope. Ask: does the rope move? Why not? Students reason that both teams pull with equal force in opposite directions. The teacher formalises: when two forces of equal magnitude act in opposite directions, the net force is zero — these are balanced forces and the object does not change its state of motion.

Working through Example 6.1 together, students analyse three configurations of a 10 N and a 6 N force acting on a block: (1) same direction — students calculate net force = 16 N and draw the resultant arrow; (2) opposite directions — students calculate net force = 4 N toward the 10 N side and mark the direction; (3) a third arrangement provided in the example. For each, students label: are forces balanced or unbalanced? What is the net force? In which direction does the object accelerate?

Pause and Ponder scenarios: (a) A weightlifter holds a barbell steady — students identify the two forces (gravity downward, applied force upward) and argue whether they are balanced. (b) In an arm-wrestling match where arms tilt toward one player — students determine which player exerted the larger force and justify using the direction of net force. Students write their reasoning in two sentences each.

Students individually create two original scenarios — one with balanced forces and one with unbalanced forces — drawn from everyday life. For each, they draw a force-arrow diagram, label the forces, state whether the net force is zero, and predict the object's motion. Pairs compare and challenge each other's diagrams.

Quick consolidation: teacher poses — 'An object moves at constant speed in a straight line. Are the forces on it balanced or unbalanced?' Students answer with justification. This plants a seed for Newton's first law, which the chapter returns to later.

periods.teacher_notes: The key conceptual target here is net force as the vector sum of all forces — not just the presence of forces. Students often think that any applied force causes motion; this unit must establish that only a non-zero net force changes the state of motion. Watch for students who add force magnitudes without attending to direction — the arm-wrestling scenario is a good diagnostic. The closing question deliberately surfaces a situation students will formalise when they reach Newton's first law.

periods.activity_title: Friction on Different Surfaces: Investigating and Measuring the Force
periods.section_anchor: 6.3 The Force of Friction: Often Overlooked but Always Present
materials: stacks of four identical coins per group
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing force directions on a pushed block: applied force, friction, gravity, normal force

time_bands.activity: Teacher places a book on the table and pushes it gently — it does not move. Ask: a force was applied; why didn't the book accelerate? Students articulate that another force opposes the push. The teacher names this friction, acting at the contact surface in the direction opposite to applied force, and draws the four-force diagram on the board: applied force, friction (horizontal), gravity (down), normal force (up).

Activity 6.1: Groups use a rubber band to launch a stack of four coins across three surfaces (wooden table, laminated surface, polished tile/marble). For each surface, students measure how far the coins travel before stopping. Results are recorded in a table: surface type vs travel distance. Groups discuss: on which surface did coins travel farthest? What does this say about friction on that surface? The class pools data and orders surfaces from highest to lowest friction.

Activity 6.2: Using a spring balance attached to a wooden block, students pull the block horizontally across each of the same surfaces. They record the spring balance reading at the moment the block just begins to move — this approximates the friction force. Students compare friction-force readings to the travel-distance order from Activity 6.1 and check for consistency: does lower friction give longer travel distance? Students write a one-paragraph conclusion connecting both activities.

Teacher poses the What If scenario: what if friction disappeared completely? Students reason through consequences in pairs — walking, stopping a car, writing with a pencil. Then the Think as a Scientist thought experiment: on a perfectly frictionless surface, would a moving coin ever slow down or stop? Students reason toward the answer: without friction there is no net horizontal force, so the coin would continue moving at constant velocity indefinitely.

Exit check: students write one sentence answering — 'Why must you continuously apply force to keep a book sliding across a real table at constant speed?' — grounding the answer in friction as an opposing force that creates a net force tending to decelerate the object.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the knowledge of friction from Grade 8 and the net-force concept established earlier in the chapter, this unit makes friction concrete and measurable. A common misconception is that an object at rest has no forces acting on it — the four-force diagram at the start directly addresses this. The thought experiment at the end is crucial: guide students to articulate that constant velocity requires zero net force, which is the statement of Newton's first law they will encounter next.

periods.activity_title: Newton's First Law: Constant Velocity, Zero Net Force, and Motion Graphs
periods.visual_aids: Board diagrams of position-time and velocity-time graphs for objects at rest and at constant velocity

time_bands.activity: The teacher restates the thought experiment conclusion from the friction investigation: on a frictionless surface, a moving object never slows. Ask: what law of motion does this suggest? Students articulate informally. The teacher then states Newton's first law formally: an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion continues at constant velocity, unless a net force acts on it. Students identify the key phrase 'unless a net force acts' and discuss what 'constant velocity' means — both constant speed AND constant direction.

Example 6.2: A moving box experiences an applied force exactly equal to friction. Students calculate the net force (zero), then predict and state the box's motion using Newton's first law. They must write a complete justification: identify both forces, confirm they balance, invoke the law, and state the outcome.

Example 6.3: Students individually draw the position-time graph and velocity-time graph for (a) an object at rest with zero net force — they should produce a horizontal line on the position-time graph and a flat line at v = 0 on the velocity-time graph; and (b) an object moving at constant velocity with zero net force — a straight sloped line on position-time, flat line at non-zero v on velocity-time. Students exchange graphs with a partner and check: does the slope of the position-time graph equal the velocity shown on the velocity-time graph?

Pause and Ponder: (a) Does a net force act on an object moving at constant velocity? Students answer with justification from Newton's first law. (b) Which of three listed states (at rest, constant velocity, constant acceleration) are possible when net force is zero? Students identify the first two. (c) Students write one real-world example of how additional applied forces produce zero net force — for instance, a book lying on a table where gravity and normal force cancel.

Consolidation: teacher poses — 'A spacecraft far from any planet moves at 8 km s⁻¹. No engines are running. Does it slow down? Explain using Newton's first law.' Students give a written one-sentence answer grounded in zero net force.

periods.teacher_notes: The transition from the frictionless thought experiment to Newton's first law is intentional: students are not receiving the law cold but confirming what their reasoning already suggested. The most persistent misconception to address is that a moving object needs a continuous force to maintain its motion — this is the Aristotelian intuition that friction reinforces in everyday life. Insist that students name the forces explicitly in every worked example before invoking the law, so they develop the habit of force analysis before conclusion.

periods.activity_title: Newton's Second Law: Reasoning from Hypothesis to F = ma
materials: slow-motion video capability (phone or tablet) if available
cardboard cart demonstration apparatus: cardboard box, wheels or rollers, thread, pulley attachment, hanging cup, masses
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of cart-and-pulley demonstration setup with labelled force arrows

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to draw on experience: if you push a shopping trolley gently and then push it hard, what is different? Students articulate that harder push produces faster acceleration. Teacher formalises the first hypothesis: for a fixed object (fixed mass), a larger net force produces a larger acceleration. Then asks the second: if you push an empty trolley and a loaded trolley with the same force, which accelerates more? Students articulate the second hypothesis: for a fixed force, a smaller mass produces larger acceleration.

Activity 6.3 demonstration: teacher sets up the cart-and-pulley system. A cup hanging from a thread pulls the cart; the cup's weight is the applied force. The travel time of the cart over a fixed distance is recorded (slow-motion video if available). The cup mass is then doubled and time recorded again. Students use the time ratio to reason about the acceleration ratio — confirming that doubling force doubles acceleration for fixed mass. Students write the result as a proportionality statement: a ∝ F (for fixed m).

Activity 6.4 demonstration: cup mass is returned to its original value (fixed force); the cart mass is doubled (e.g., by adding a second identical box or mass). Time is again recorded. Students compare times and calculate the acceleration ratio — confirming that doubling mass halves acceleration for fixed force. Students write: a ∝ 1/m (for fixed F). The teacher combines both proportionalities: a ∝ F/m, so F = ma, and formally states Newton's second law in words and equation.

Students derive the SI definition of one newton from F = ma: the force that produces 1 m s⁻² acceleration on a 1 kg mass. They then derive F = mg by applying Newton's second law to a freely falling object (acceleration = g = 9.8 m s⁻²), and calculate the weight of a 30 kg barbell (Example 6.4), confirming the weightlifter must apply 294 N upward to hold it stationary.

Exit question: 'Why does a fielder pull their hands backward when catching a fast cricket ball?' Students apply Newton's second law qualitatively: increasing the time of deceleration reduces the acceleration, which reduces the force experienced — a direct application of F = ma.

periods.teacher_notes: The deliberate move from hypothesis to demonstration to equation prevents the law from arriving as a formula to memorise. Students frequently confuse larger mass with larger acceleration; the second demonstration directly challenges this. Emphasise that F in F = ma is the NET force — a point that trips students in every worked example; a student who writes F = ma but uses only the applied force (ignoring friction) is applying the formula incorrectly.

periods.activity_title: Applying F = ma: Worked Problems and Velocity-Time Graph Analysis
periods.visual_aids: Velocity-time graph for the sports car (Example 6.6) drawn on the board with three labelled intervals

time_bands.activity: Example 6.5: A block on the floor is pushed with 50 N. Friction is 50 N. Students apply Newton's second law: net force = 0 N, so the block does not accelerate — it stays at rest (Newton's first law confirms this). The problem is then varied: push is 55 N, friction is still 50 N. Students calculate net force (5 N), mass (given), acceleration, and use kinematics to find displacement after 2 s. The teacher requires students to show each step: identify forces → compute net force → apply F = ma → apply kinematics.

Example 6.6: Students are given the velocity-time graph for a 1500 kg sports car across three time intervals. For each interval, students (a) read the slope to find acceleration, (b) apply F = ma to find the net force, and (c) determine the direction of the net force relative to motion. Results: accelerating phase (3000 N forward), constant-velocity phase (0 N net force), braking phase (−3000 N, i.e., 3000 N opposing motion). Students annotate the graph with force values and directions.

Pause and Ponder set: (a) Net force on a toy car moving at constant velocity — students state zero and justify. (b) Two children of different masses on identical swings requiring the same acceleration — students use F = ma to determine which child needs larger force and explain. (c) Why does bubble wrap or hay protect fragile glass items in transport? Students apply the same reasoning as the fielder-catching scenario: increased deformation time reduces acceleration and force. Students write complete sentences for each.

Students work individually on a short synthesis problem (teacher-constructed or textbook): a 20 kg box is pushed with 80 N; friction is 40 N. Students find net force, acceleration, and velocity after 3 s. Then they sketch the velocity-time graph for those 3 s. Pairs check each other's graphs.

Consolidation: teacher asks — 'In Example 6.6, during the constant-velocity phase, are there zero forces on the car, or balanced forces? Explain.' Students must distinguish zero net force from zero force — reinforcing that balanced forces (engine thrust equals drag) produce zero net force, not absence of force.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit consolidates the F = ma relationship through problem-solving after the law was established in the demonstration unit. The most productive error to surface and correct is students applying F = ma with the applied force alone rather than the net force — Examples 6.5 and the synthesis problem both create this opportunity. The closing question deliberately revisits Newton's first law in a Newton's second law context, reinforcing that the two laws are consistent descriptions of the same physical reality.
homework: A 5 kg block rests on a surface. A force of 30 N is applied horizontally; friction on the block is 18 N. Calculate the net force and the acceleration of the block, then sketch the velocity-time graph for the first 4 seconds of motion.

periods.activity_title: Newton's Third Law: Force Pairs, Equal Magnitudes, and the Wheeled-Chair Test
materials: two identical spring balances connected hook-to-hook (Activity 6.6)
inflated balloon, straw, taut string, tape (Activity 6.7)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing action-reaction force pairs for walking, rowing, and rocket examples with labelled arrows on two separate objects

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses: if you push a wall, does the wall push back? Students vote and give reasons. The teacher states Newton's third law: whenever object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts an equal and opposite force on object A. Emphasise: the force pair acts on TWO DIFFERENT objects — they do not cancel. The teacher draws the walking example on the board: foot pushes ground backward (action); friction from ground pushes person forward (reaction) — two arrows on two different objects.

Activity 6.5: A student sits on a wheeled chair and pushes a heavy table. The class observes the direction the chair moves. The student then pulls the table. The class observes the direction again. Students draw force-arrow diagrams for both push and pull cases, labelling which force is on the table and which is on the student-chair system. Key question: why does the chair move at all if it is the student doing the pushing?

Activity 6.6: Two identical spring balances are connected hook-to-hook on a flat surface. Students take turns pulling from each end with different magnitudes of force. Each time, they read both balances simultaneously and record. Students tabulate their results: do the readings ever differ? They conclude that the force magnitudes are always equal, confirming the equal-magnitude clause of Newton's third law.

Activity 6.7: Balloon-and-straw rocket. Students thread a straw onto a taut string, attach an inflated balloon to the straw, and release the balloon's neck. Students observe the direction of balloon motion versus the direction of escaping air, draw a force-pair diagram, and connect to rocket propulsion: exhaust expelled downward, reaction force pushes rocket upward. The teacher mentions Chandrayaan-3's reverse thrust for soft landing.

Students work through Examples 6.7 and 6.8: (6.7) Earth and a falling fruit exert equal gravitational forces on each other — students calculate that Earth's acceleration is negligibly small due to its enormous mass; (6.8) a 0.1 kg bullet and 5 kg gun both experience a 2 N force — students calculate each acceleration (20 m s⁻² and 0.4 m s⁻²) and explain the difference using Newton's second law.

Pause and Ponder exit: students explain in two sentences why a firefighter struggles to hold a water-issuing hose, using Newton's third law. They also suggest how a spacecraft in negligible gravity can change its velocity — connecting to the rocket/balloon activity.

periods.teacher_notes: The single most persistent error with Newton's third law is treating the action-reaction pair as forces that cancel, producing zero net force. This must be directly named and corrected: the two forces act on different objects and can never cancel because cancellation requires forces on the same object. The spring-balance activity (Activity 6.6) is particularly powerful because students expect the balance being 'pulled harder' to read more — empirical data corrects this directly.

periods.activity_title: Newton's Third Law: Contact, Non-Contact, and Real-World Applications
materials: two similarly charged balloons (rubbed on wool)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of magnet-repulsion and balloon-repulsion force-pair arrows; diagram of Chandrayaan-3 reverse-thrust configuration

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds two magnets near each other — students observe repulsion without contact and are asked: does Newton's third law apply here? Students predict, then the teacher pushes one magnet toward the other and releases; both accelerate away. Students draw force-pair arrows: magnet A pushes magnet B to the right; magnet B simultaneously pushes magnet A to the left. The same is shown with two similarly charged suspended balloons. The class concludes: the third law applies equally to contact and non-contact forces.

Teacher-led worked analysis of four real-world third-law applications from the chapter: (1) walking — foot on ground backward, ground on foot forward; (2) rowing a canoe — paddle on water backward, water on paddle forward; (3) climbing a coconut tree — legs push trunk down, trunk friction pushes person up; (4) rocket — exhaust expelled downward, reaction pushes rocket upward. For each, students must identify the TWO objects forming the force pair and state the direction of each force. They record all four in a structured table: Object A | Force on B | Object B | Force on A.

Students apply the third law to the airbag and seat-belt context from the chapter's real-world section: in a collision, the car decelerates rapidly; an unrestrained passenger continues forward (Newton's first law) and hits the dashboard. The airbag inflates, extending the deceleration time — students apply Newton's second law to show this reduces force. They then identify the third-law pair when the passenger pushes into the airbag (passenger pushes bag; bag pushes passenger backward). Students write a connected two-law explanation.

Students work in pairs on a novel scenario: a person stands on a skateboard and throws a heavy ball forward. Using Newton's third law, they predict the direction the skateboard moves; using Newton's second law, they explain qualitatively why the skateboard accelerates less than the ball. They draw force diagrams and write two justifying sentences.

Consolidation: teacher asks — 'If two ice-skaters of very different masses push off each other, which one moves faster after the push? Explain using Newton's third and second laws together.' Students give a spoken or written answer connecting equal force (third law) and unequal mass → unequal acceleration (second law).

periods.teacher_notes: After the hands-on confirmation of the third law, this unit builds conceptual breadth by extending the law to non-contact forces and diverse real-world applications. Students sometimes think Newton's third law only applies when objects are touching — the magnet and balloon demonstrations directly challenge this. The airbag analysis is a rich moment to show how the three laws operate simultaneously in one scenario; encourage students to name which law they are invoking in each step of their explanation.

periods.activity_title: Forces on a System of Objects: Internal Forces, External Force, and Net Acceleration
periods.section_anchor: 6.7 Forces Acting on a System of Objects
materials: two labelled blocks (m₁ and m₂) for demonstration or diagram
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of two connected boxes on a frictionless surface pulled by external force F, with internal tension T labelled

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws two boxes (m₁ = 3 kg, m₂ = 5 kg) connected by a string on a frictionless surface, pulled by external force F = 16 N. Ask: how would you find the acceleration of the system? Students attempt the problem individually. Some will try to apply F = ma to each box separately (needing tension T); some may try F = ma to the whole system. Both approaches are collected on the board.

Teacher develops the system approach formally. Define the system as both boxes plus the string. Internal forces (tension) act within the system and, by Newton's third law, cancel in pairs — they do not contribute to the system's acceleration. Only the external force F matters. Applying Newton's second law to the system: a = F/(m₁ + m₂) = 16/8 = 2 m s⁻². Students verify this is identical to the result obtained by the longer individual-object analysis. The teacher emphasises: the system approach is not a shortcut trick but a direct application of Newton's second law to the total mass of the system under external forces only.

Students work through two variations: (a) F = 24 N, m₁ = 4 kg, m₂ = 8 kg — find acceleration; (b) a = 3 m s⁻², m₁ = 2 kg, m₂ = 4 kg — find the external force needed. For each, students must write: define the system → identify external force → identify total mass → apply a = F_net/m_total. Pairs cross-check their working.

Students consider a three-box system (m₁, m₂, m₃) pulled by force F on a frictionless surface and are asked to write the expression for acceleration and explain, using Newton's third law, why the tensions between boxes do not appear in the system-level equation. This extends the pattern to an arbitrary number of connected objects.

Exit check: 'A locomotive of mass M pulls two identical carriages each of mass m, with net force F, on frictionless tracks. What is the acceleration of the train?' Students write the expression a = F/(M + 2m) and state which forces were ignored and why.

periods.teacher_notes: The system approach is conceptually richer than it appears — it requires students to apply Newton's third law (internal forces cancel) and Newton's second law (to the total mass under external force) simultaneously. The most common error is including the tension in the net-force calculation when using the system method; insisting that students explicitly label which forces are internal before applying the equation prevents this. The three-box extension at the end is an open-ended probe of whether students understand the principle, not just the two-box formula.

periods.activity_title: Airbags, Treads, and Tyre Grooves: Newton's Laws in Everyday Safety Design
periods.section_anchor: 6.7 Forces Acting on a System of Objects
materials: printed or projected images of airbag deployment, tyre tread patterns, grooved shoe soles
periods.visual_aids: Projected or printed images of airbag cross-section and tyre tread; board diagram of force-time graph showing long vs short deceleration intervals

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows two images: a tyre with deep treads and a bald tyre; a shoe with grooved sole and a smooth-soled shoe. Ask: which is safer on a wet surface, and why? Students reason from their knowledge of friction from the investigation unit — grooves increase the contact texture and friction coefficient. The teacher then draws out: the same physics that we measured with wooden blocks on surfaces explains why vehicle and shoe design matters.

Students are given the airbag scenario in the chapter's real-world section. In groups, they construct a chain of reasoning connecting three laws: (1) Newton's first law explains why an unrestrained passenger continues moving forward when the car stops; (2) Newton's second law (F = ma, or equivalently F = m·Δv/Δt) explains how increasing Δt by inflating the airbag reduces F; (3) Newton's third law identifies the reaction force the airbag exerts on the passenger. Each group writes their chain on the board in three labelled steps.

Discovery extension: teacher asks — 'Why do footballers wear studded boots? Why do racing cars use slick tyres on dry tracks but grooved tyres in rain?' Students reason from friction principles: studs penetrate soft ground to increase resistance; slick tyres maximise contact area on dry tarmac for grip; grooves channel water away on wet surfaces to restore contact. Students draw and annotate diagrams for each case.

Students connect walking and running (Newton's third law: foot pushes ground backward, friction pushes person forward) to the grooved-sole design. They write a short explanation (three to four sentences) of how a grooved sole on a wet floor prevents slipping, using Newton's third law to identify the force pair and friction to explain the magnitude of the forward force.

Consolidation: teacher poses — 'A car travelling at 60 km/h brakes on a wet road and takes 8 m to stop. On a dry road it takes 4 m. Explain the difference using the concept of friction and Newton's second law.' Students give a two-sentence qualitative answer.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses real-world safety design as the discovery vehicle to consolidate all three of Newton's laws in a single applied context — the chapter's own real-world application section supplies the content. Students sometimes treat the airbag, tyre, and sole examples as separate unrelated facts; the group task of writing the three-law chain makes the connections explicit. Probe whether students can correctly identify the third-law pair in the airbag scenario (passenger-on-bag and bag-on-passenger) rather than confusing it with the car's deceleration.

periods.activity_title: Velocity-Time Graphs and Force Analysis: Multi-Section Problem Solving
periods.visual_aids: A multi-interval velocity-time graph drawn on the board with three distinct phases: acceleration, constant velocity, deceleration

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a novel velocity-time graph on the board — a 2500 kg truck, four time intervals: 0–5 s (velocity increases from 0 to 10 m/s), 5–10 s (constant at 10 m/s), 10–14 s (velocity increases from 10 to 18 m/s), 14–18 s (velocity decreases to 0). Students individually calculate the acceleration for each interval from the graph's slope.

Students apply F = ma to each interval: calculate net force magnitude and direction for all four phases. For the constant-velocity phase they invoke Newton's first law (net force = 0) and discuss what engine force and friction must be doing. For the braking phase they determine the direction of net force is opposite to motion and identify that this is the braking/friction force. Students annotate their graphs with net force values and arrows.

Extension analysis: in the braking phase (14–18 s), students are asked — 'If the braking force is friction between tyres and road, and the truck has four tyres each contributing equally, what friction force does each tyre provide?' This connects to the system concept (Section 6.7) and requires students to divide the total net force by four. Students write a complete solution with units.

Students design their own velocity-time graph for a hypothetical object of given mass, specifying at least three phases. For each phase they calculate the required net force. They then swap graphs with a partner, who calculates the forces independently. Pairs reconcile any discrepancies.

Closing discussion: teacher asks — 'On a velocity-time graph, what feature tells you the direction of net force, and what feature tells you there is no net force?' Students articulate: positive slope → net force in direction of motion; negative slope → net force opposing motion; zero slope (flat line) → zero net force.

periods.teacher_notes: Velocity-time graph analysis of forces is a site where students confuse the sign of acceleration with the direction of velocity — in the braking phase, velocity is positive but acceleration is negative, meaning net force opposes motion. Spend time explicitly distinguishing direction of velocity from direction of net force. The per-tyre friction calculation is an informal introduction to distributed forces and connects naturally to the system approach developed in Section 6.7.

periods.activity_title: Predict, Justify, Connect: Applying All Three Newton's Laws to Novel Scenarios
periods.section_anchor: 6.7 Forces Acting on a System of Objects
materials: printed scenario cards (one per group) or teacher-read scenarios
graph paper if needed for any calculation
periods.visual_aids: Board summary table: Law | Statement | Key Condition | Example — filled in collaboratively at the start

time_bands.activity: The class collaboratively builds a summary table on the board: each row covers one Newton's law — its statement, the key physical condition it describes, and one example from the chapter. Students contribute one item per row from memory. The teacher corrects and completes. This is not a review for its own sake but a shared reference students use during the scenario work that follows.

Groups of three receive a novel scenario card (teacher-prepared). Each scenario is explicitly multi-law: e.g., 'A 4 kg skateboard with a 60 kg rider at rest. The rider throws a 2 kg ball forward at 5 m/s. (a) Identify the third-law force pair when the ball is thrown. (b) Using the system approach (rider + skateboard), find the recoil acceleration. (c) Once the ball is in the air and no other horizontal forces act, describe the ball's subsequent motion.' Groups work out their scenario fully: draw force diagrams, apply the relevant law for each sub-question, and prepare to present.

Two or three groups present their scenario solutions to the class. The class asks questions and the teacher probes: 'Which forces are internal to your system? Which are external? How does Newton's third law tell you the forces are equal even though the accelerations differ?' Misconceptions are corrected during discussion.

Individual written task: students choose any one real-world application from the chapter — walking, a rocket, catching a ball, an airbag — and write a three-paragraph explanation connecting all three Newton's laws to that application. Each paragraph explicitly names the law, states the condition it applies to, and describes the physical outcome.

Closing question: 'A 70 kg astronaut on a space station (no gravity, no air) pushes off a 500 kg wall with 350 N for 0.2 s. What is the astronaut's velocity after the push? Which law tells you the wall exerted 350 N on the astronaut, and which law gives you the acceleration?' Students write the answer, naming the laws by number.

periods.teacher_notes: The scenario card task is designed to require students to identify which law applies to each sub-question before calculating — this is the capstone skill the chapter develops. A common error is applying Newton's third law to explain why an object does not accelerate (confusing it with balanced forces under the first law); the mixed scenarios make this confusion visible and correctable in the group setting. The individual writing task at the end checks whether students can articulate the laws in their own words, not just use them numerically.

questions.question_text: A goalkeeper kicks a stationary football with a certain force and it moves in a particular direction. The goalkeeper then kicks an identical stationary football with the same magnitude of force but in the opposite direction. Which statement correctly describes the outcome of the second kick compared with the first?

options.label: A
options.text: The ball does not move because equal and opposite forces balance each other.

options.label: B
options.text: The ball moves in the opposite direction because the direction of the force has changed.

options.label: C
options.text: The ball moves in the same direction as the first kick because the force magnitude is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: The ball moves in the same direction as the first kick but with lower speed because force is a scalar.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student treats force as a scalar — recognises magnitude but ignores direction as a determinant of the effect.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses Newton's third law force pairs (which act on different objects) with balanced forces on one object; or conflates the two kicks as simultaneous forces on the same ball.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student holds the misconception that force is a scalar quantity and incorrectly predicts a speed change rather than a direction change.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who draw vector arrows rather than write a verbal answer demonstrate the same understanding; accept labelled diagrams as full responses. Students who verbalise 'the kick pushed it the other way' with a directional gesture are showing the concept even if they lack the vocabulary.

questions.question_text: A student uses a spring balance to measure the weight of a 0.5 kg stone and records the reading in newtons. (a) State what physical quantity the spring balance is measuring when the stone hangs from its hook, and explain in one sentence why weight is a force. (b) The same spring balance is then used to pull a wooden block horizontally across a table. Explain whether the spring balance can still give a valid force reading in this new orientation, and what it now measures. (c) A laboratory instrument can detect a force of 3 × 10⁻²¹ N. Express this force in yoctonewtons (1 yoctonewton = 10⁻²⁴ N) and state how many times larger it is than 1 yoctonewton.
expected_elements: (a) The spring balance measures the gravitational force (weight) with which Earth pulls the stone; weight is a force because it is an interaction between two objects (Earth and the stone) that can change the stone's state of motion or shape.

(b) The spring balance can still give a valid force reading in any orientation; it now measures the magnitude of the horizontal force applied to pull the block — demonstrating that a spring balance measures any force applied to it, not only weight.
(c) 3 × 10⁻²¹ N ÷ 10⁻²⁴ N/yN = 3 × 10³ yoctonewtons = 3000 yoctonewtons; this is 3000 times larger than 1 yoctonewton.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who express part (a) in everyday language ('the spring pulls against gravity') still demonstrate the concept if they correctly identify the interaction; award partial credit. For part (c), students who correctly set up the division but make an arithmetic error in the power of ten should receive credit for method.

questions.question_text: Refer to the table provided. Three configurations (P, Q, R) show two forces acting on a block. Which row correctly identifies the net force and the expected motion of the block for configuration Q?

options.label: A
options.text: Net force = 0 N; the block does not accelerate.

options.label: B
options.text: Net force = 16 N in the direction of the 10 N force; the block accelerates.

options.label: C
options.text: Net force = 4 N in the direction of the 10 N force; the block accelerates.

options.label: D
options.text: Net force = 4 N in the direction of the 6 N force; the block accelerates.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student added the magnitudes instead of subtracting for opposite-direction forces, ignoring the vector nature of force.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly subtracted magnitudes but reversed the direction — assigned net force to the smaller force rather than the larger.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student recognised opposite directions and assumed the forces must cancel, without checking whether magnitudes are equal; confuses configuration Q with configuration R.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who draw force arrows and correctly label the resultant direction but write the wrong arithmetic value should receive partial credit; the directional reasoning is the key skill. Students who annotate the table rather than answer in prose demonstrate equivalent understanding.

questions.visual_stimulus:
Surface | Coin travel distance (cm) | Spring balance reading when block just moves (N)
Wooden table | 18 | 2.4
Laminated surface | 27 | 1.6
Polished marble | 41 | 1.0
questions.question_text: Refer to the table provided, which shows results from Activities 6.1 and 6.2 for three surfaces. (a) State the relationship between coin travel distance and the friction force measured by the spring balance, as shown by the data. (b) Explain, using the concept of net force, why the coin decelerates and stops on the wooden table after the rubber band launches it. (c) A student imagines a fourth surface where friction is exactly zero. Predict what the coin's motion would be after launch on this surface, and justify your prediction using the concept of net force.
expected_elements: (a) As friction force (spring balance reading) decreases, coin travel distance increases — surfaces with lower friction allow the coin to travel farther before stopping; the data show an inverse relationship between friction force and travel distance.

(b) Once launched, the only horizontal force on the coin is friction acting opposite to its direction of motion; this unbalanced net force decelerates the coin (Newton's second law / net force causes acceleration in the direction of the force) until the coin stops.

(c) On a frictionless surface there is no horizontal net force on the launched coin; by Newton's first law (or zero-net-force reasoning), the coin would continue moving at the same velocity indefinitely and would never stop.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who provide correct reasoning for parts (b) and (c) using everyday language ('nothing is slowing it down') rather than technical terms still demonstrate the principle; look for the causal chain (no friction → no opposing force → no deceleration) as the criterion. For part (a), a correctly drawn graph of the two columns in lieu of a verbal statement is fully acceptable.

questions.question_text: A 4 kg box moves along a smooth horizontal surface. An applied force of 12 N acts on the box in the forward direction, and a friction force of 12 N acts in the backward direction. (a) Calculate the net force on the box and state what Newton's first law predicts for the box's motion. (b) Sketch the shape of the velocity-time graph for this box over a 5-second interval, assuming it was already moving at 3 m/s at t = 0. Label the axes and the value of velocity. (c) On a separate set of axes, sketch the position-time graph for the same 5-second interval. Explain in one sentence how the slope of the position-time graph is related to the velocity-time graph you drew.
expected_elements: (a) Net force = 12 N − 12 N = 0 N; Newton's first law predicts the box continues moving at constant velocity (3 m/s) in the forward direction — it neither accelerates nor decelerates.
(b) Velocity-time graph: a horizontal straight line at v = 3 m/s from t = 0 to t = 5 s; axes labelled velocity (m/s) on y-axis and time (s) on x-axis.

(c) Position-time graph: a straight line with positive constant slope starting from the initial position; the slope of the position-time graph equals the constant velocity (3 m/s) shown as the flat line on the velocity-time graph.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who draw correct graph shapes but mislabel axis units demonstrate graphical reasoning; award most credit and note the labelling gap. Students who correctly identify net force as zero and invoke the first law verbally without sketching the graph should be given credit for the law application and guided on the graphical representation separately.

questions.visual_stimulus:
Time interval (s) | Velocity at start (m/s) | Velocity at end (m/s)
0–4 | 0 | 12
4–10 | 12 | 12
10–14 | 12 | 20
14–17 | 20 | 2
questions.question_text: A 1200 kg car moves along a straight road. The table provided shows its velocity at the start and end of four time intervals. (a) For each time interval, calculate the acceleration and the net force on the car. Clearly indicate the direction of the net force relative to the car's motion. (b) In the interval from 4–10 s, the car's engine is still running and producing a forward thrust. Explain what this tells you about the friction and air resistance during that interval, using Newton's first law and Newton's second law together. (c) During the interval 14–17 s, the car is decelerating to a near-stop. A passenger of mass 60 kg is in the car. Using Newton's second law, calculate the force the seat exerts on the passenger during this interval, and state its direction. Then explain qualitatively why a seat belt is important during this deceleration.
look_for: Part (a): Correct accelerations — 3 m/s², 0 m/s², 2 m/s², −6 m/s² — and corresponding net forces — 3600 N forward, 0 N, 2400 N forward, 7200 N backward — with direction stated for each.

Part (b): Explicit invocation of Newton's first law (zero net force → constant velocity) to establish that net force = 0 in the 4–10 s interval; then Newton's second law applied to conclude that engine thrust equals the sum of friction and air resistance (resistive forces) exactly — not that these forces are absent.

Part (c): Correct calculation: acceleration = (2 − 20)/(17 − 14) = −6 m/s²; force on passenger = 60 × (−6) = −360 N, i.e., 360 N backward (opposing forward motion); qualitative explanation that without a seat belt the passenger continues forward at 20 m/s (Newton's first law) while the car decelerates, risking impact — the seat belt applies the backward force needed to decelerate the passenger with the car.
Cross-law reasoning: student names which law applies to which sub-question and does not confuse zero net force with zero force, nor action-reaction pairs with balanced forces.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who present correct reasoning in annotated diagrams or tables rather than continuous prose should receive full credit if the causal chain is clear. Students who correctly complete parts (a) and (c) numerically but struggle with part (b)'s verbal reasoning demonstrate computational competency; note the analytical gap. Students for whom English is not the primary language of reasoning should be assessed on the logical structure of their argument rather than grammatical form.

questions.question_text: A 0.1 kg bullet is fired from a 4 kg rifle. The explosive gases exert a force of 800 N on the bullet for a brief interval. Which of the following correctly applies Newton's third law to this situation?

options.label: A
options.text: The bullet and rifle exert equal forces on each other, so the net force on the bullet-rifle system is zero and neither moves.

options.label: B
options.text: The force on the bullet is 800 N forward and the force on the rifle is 800 N forward, because both objects experience the same explosive force.

options.label: C
options.text: The rifle exerts 800 N on the bullet (forward) and the bullet exerts 800 N on the rifle (backward); the bullet accelerates more than the rifle because it has less mass.

options.label: D
options.text: The rifle exerts 800 N on the bullet (forward) and the bullet exerts a smaller force on the rifle because the rifle is heavier.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student conflates force magnitude with mass — believes heavier objects receive smaller reaction forces; directly contradicts the equal-magnitude clause of Newton's third law.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student correctly identifies equal forces but incorrectly concludes neither object moves — confuses Newton's third law pairs (acting on different objects) with balanced forces (acting on the same object); the classic third-law misconception.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses the source of the force — assigns the same direction to both forces, ignoring that the reaction force on the rifle is in the opposite direction to the action force on the bullet.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who draw labelled force-pair diagrams with arrows on two separate objects rather than selecting an option demonstrate equivalent reasoning; accept annotated diagrams as responses. Students who reason correctly in words ('the lighter one moves faster') but cannot formally state the law should receive credit for the conceptual reasoning.

questions.question_text: A 70 kg person stands on a 200 kg raft floating on still water. She pushes a 5 kg box horizontally off the raft with a force of 50 N. (a) Identify the Newton's third law force pair that acts when she pushes the box, naming both objects clearly. (b) Explain in one sentence why this force pair does not result in zero net motion for either object. (c) Calculate the acceleration of the box and the acceleration of the person-raft system at the instant of the push. Assume no friction from water.
expected_elements: (a) The person exerts a 50 N force on the box (in the direction the box is pushed); simultaneously the box exerts a 50 N force on the person in the opposite direction — these are the Newton's third law pair, acting on two different objects.
(b) The two forces act on different objects (one on the box, one on the person-raft system) and therefore cannot cancel each other — cancellation would require both forces to act on the same object.
(c) Acceleration of box = F/m = 50/5 = 10 m/s² in the direction of push; acceleration of person-raft system = F/m = 50/(70 + 200) = 50/270 ≈ 0.185 m/s² in the opposite direction.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who correctly name the force pair and explain the cancellation issue in everyday language ('they push on different things') demonstrate the conceptual core; full credit for the reasoning even if formal language is absent. For part (c), students who correctly identify the system mass as 270 kg but make an arithmetic slip should receive most marks for the method.

questions.task:
Two crates, A (mass 6 kg) and B (mass 10 kg), are connected by a string on a frictionless horizontal surface. A horizontal force F is applied to crate A. The velocity of crate A (and therefore of the whole connected system) is recorded in the table provided.

Using the data and the system approach to Newton's second law:
(1) Calculate the acceleration of the system during the intervals 0–6 s and 8–14 s.
(2) Determine the external force F during each interval.
(3) During the interval 0–6 s, explain why the tension in the string between A and B does NOT appear in the system-level calculation, using Newton's third law to justify your reasoning.
(4) A second student argues: 'During the interval 8–14 s, the force F must be acting backward on A to make it decelerate.' Evaluate this claim. Is it correct? If not, identify an alternative explanation consistent with the data and Newton's laws.
questions.scaffold:
For tasks (1) and (2): define your system first (which objects are in it?), then identify only the external force(s), then apply a = F_net / m_total.
For task (3): think about what Newton's third law says about the tension that A exerts on B and the tension that B exerts on A — what happens to these forces at the system level?
For task (4): use the velocity-time data to determine the direction of acceleration, then reason from Newton's second law about the direction of the net force.
format_of_output: Numerical working for accelerations and forces with correct units
A written explanation (3–5 sentences) for task (3) naming Newton's third law explicitly
A written evaluation (3–5 sentences) for task (4) stating whether the claim is correct and providing the correct explanation

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Data interpretation (provided table) combined with procedure evaluation
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The section's core skill is applying Newton's second law to a system by reading acceleration from a velocity-time table and distinguishing internal from external forces; data interpretation from the table drives tasks (1)–(3), while task (4) is a procedure/claim evaluation — the most natural vehicle for the section's analytical and evaluative demand.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students demonstrate that they can extract kinematic information from tabular data, apply the system approach to Newton's second law (identifying external forces and total mass), invoke Newton's third law to explain why internal forces cancel at the system level, and critically evaluate a claim about force direction using evidence from the data.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts students to define the system before calculating, which is the critical first step in the system approach — students who skip this step often include tension as an external force. For task (4), the scaffold directs students to the velocity-time data first, preventing the common error of evaluating the claim on intuition alone rather than on the sign of acceleration.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: explicitly state the system boundary and total mass before calculating; correctly identify 1.5 m/s² and −1.5 m/s² accelerations and corresponding forces of 24 N and −24 N; explain internal force cancellation by naming that tension on B by A and tension on A by B are equal and opposite (Newton's third law) and act within the system; evaluate the claim in task (4) by noting velocity is decreasing but still positive, so acceleration is negative (net force opposes motion), and identify that F is removed or a braking force acts — not that F reverses. Weak responses: include tension in the system force equation; state net force is zero because the system 'eventually stops'; evaluate task (4) by restating the claim without using the velocity-time data.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who present correct numerical working in table form rather than prose equations should receive full credit. Students who correctly reason through tasks (3) and (4) verbally but make arithmetic errors in (1) and (2) demonstrate the higher-order skills targeted by this item; assess reasoning and calculation separately. Students who sketch a velocity-time graph from the table as a preliminary step demonstrate an additional representational skill and should be credited for it.
